title: Sexual Assaults on Campus No Longer Scrutinized as Closely Under Trump’s Education Department
author: Jodi S. Cohen
content:
The civil rights arm of the U.S. Department of Education has dramatically
scaled back investigations involving schools and colleges since the second
Trump administration began, even as complaints continue to pour in, a
ProPublica analysis of newly obtained records found.

The analysis shows how severely the department’s Office for Civil Rights has
retracted from its mission, launching an average of about 100 new
investigations a month — 1,839 total from Inauguration Day in 2025 through
July 2026. The OCR launched an average of 310 new investigations each month in
2024 during the Biden administration, according to data previously obtained by
ProPublica.

Under President Donald Trump, the OCR abandoned the [public-facing list of
schools it was investigating and the reasons for those
investigations](https://ocrcas.ed.gov/open-
investigations?field_ois_state=All&field_ois_discrimination_statute=All&field_ois_type_of_discrimination=727&items_per_page=20&field_ois_institution=&field_ois_institution_type=All&field_open_investigation_date_1=2024-01-01%2000%3A00%3A00&field_open_investigation_date_2=2025-01-01%2023%3A59%3A59&field_open_investigation_date=&field_open_investigation_date_3=&field_open_investigation_dat_1=2026-10-15%2000%3A00%3A00&field_open_investigation_dat_2=2026-10-15%2023%3A59%3A59&page=2),
including claims of discrimination based on race, sex and disability.
[ProPublica sued the department](https://www.propublica.org/article/education-
department-civil-rights-office-foia-lawsuit) to obtain internal case data. The
government subsequently provided records of the OCR’s actions in the first 18
months of Trump’s return to power, and we are publishing the data so the
public can search the cases.

The OCR uses “case opened” to record when complaints were received by the

The decline in investigations is especially dramatic for cases involving sex
discrimination. More than 200 new complaints were filed with the office
related to schools’ handling of sexual violence — rape, assault and abuse. But
the Trump administration launched investigations in only 29 of them, finding
fault with a school district only once, according to the newly obtained data.
It’s typical for there to be at least 60 sexual violence investigations opened
each year.

The department addressed fewer of these cases despite continued concerns about
the persistence of the problem — as demonstrated by the intense public
scrutiny over how Cornell University addressed a student’s report of a 2024
gang rape.

Beyond that, the OCR launched only two investigations into discrimination
based on sexual orientation.

“They’re barely doing anything to protect women and girls, including survivors
of sexual violence,” said Shiwali Patel, an attorney who previously worked at
the OCR and is now with the National Women’s Law Center. “They just don’t care
about women and girls.”

The organization and more than 120 other advocacy, civil rights and education
groups sent a letter on Tuesday to Congress’ ranking education committee
leaders urging them to hold the OCR accountable for “its failure to enforce
civil rights law and protect students from sexual violence.”

With OCR’s online database idle since Trump took office, the only way to know
where the agency has launched investigations has been through selective
department press releases, when OCR employees provided internal data to
reporters or from schools and colleges that acknowledged that their
institutions had become targets of the investigations.

The data ProPublica received as a result of our lawsuit can now fill that gap
on the more than 1,800 civil rights investigations that the department
initiated from Jan. 20, 2025, to July 29 of this year. The database also
reflects the 24,000 new complaints logged through May and the nearly 17,000
new and old cases the department closed — almost always by dismissing them.

The agency is dismissing complaints more frequently than in prior years, the
records show. And fewer than 700 cases opened by the administration were
resolved with a finding of wrongdoing.

The data does not include investigations that had been opened before Trump
retook power but that are pending decisions by OCR — a backlog of more than
10,000 cases.

In response to questions from ProPublica, an Education Department spokesperson
blamed the Biden administration for leaving office with 19,000 unresolved
cases, which the Trump administration has worked to address.

“Spare us the crocodile tears as the Trump Administration is working to
restore OCR to its original purpose: enforcing the law to ensure all students
can receive an education free from discrimination,” spokesperson Sabin Sidney
wrote.

He added that the administration “treats any form of discrimination on the
basis of race or sex as illegal.” And he criticized the prior administration
for endorsing policies that allowed transgender girls and women to compete in
women’s athletics and use women's restrooms.

The data disclosure comes as the administration is moving forward with efforts
to shut down the department and move the OCR under the Department of Justice.
Disability rights advocates and others have been critical of the move, while
the administration says it will lead to more efficiency and do a better job
protecting students’ rights. The majority of cases before the OCR involve
students with disabilities, as has been the case historically.

In the early months of Trump’s second term, Education Secretary Linda McMahon
[fired hundreds of employees](https://www.propublica.org/article/education-
department-civil-rights-division-eroded-by-massive-layoffs) and closed seven
regional OCR offices, leaving the department severely diminished. Its
remaining civil rights workers have described untenable case loads and
pressure to dismiss complaints.

The remaining attorneys “are navigating pure chaos,” said Rachel Gittleman,
president of the American Federation of Government Employees Local 252, the
union that represents OCR staff. “They are being asked to use the tools they
have used for their entire careers not for good, not to protect students, but
to harm students. You see it in the case dismissals, the cases that target
trans students or people of color.”

In examining the new records, ProPublica found the extent to which the agency
has shifted its focus, as the OCR places a new emphasis on complaints that men
faced discrimination. The agency launched 172 investigations into alleged
“discrimination against males,” compared with 104 cases of alleged
“discrimination against females” in the period examined.

It also has investigated allegations that campus programs or scholarships
excluded men. For example, it investigated a complaint against Skyline College
in California that had been filed in 2023 but that President Joe Biden’s
administration had not acted on, according to records from the university. The
complaint alleged that Skyline discriminated against men by listing
scholarships on its website that are exclusively for women and for promoting a
program for women.

The civil rights office opened the investigation in mid-April, and two weeks
later the community college agreed that it would remove the scholarships from
its website and add language that the program was open to all students. A
Skyline College spokesperson did not respond to questions from ProPublica.

At the same time, the agency chose to open fewer than 370 new investigations
involving racial discrimination, even though about 5,000 complaints were
filed.

Of those new investigations, about 11% involved allegations of discrimination
against white students. Over the summer, the department announced
investigations into five medical schools’ admissions policies.

“They are not allocating their resources to racial discrimination complaints,
to sexual assault complaints, to the types of complaints that really often
speak to systematic discrimination and problems,” said Johnathan Smith,
managing director of education at the nonprofit National Center for Youth Law.

That organization also has sued the Education Department for similar
information obtained by ProPublica; the lawsuit is pending.

### How We Analyzed the Data

We received two data files from the U.S. Department of Education — one file
contained Office for Civil Rights cases that were initiated through a
complaint or had a resolution from Jan. 20, 2025, through July 2026. The other
listed investigation notices sent to institutions from Jan. 20, 2025, through
April 9, 2026. Most Trump administration investigations started with a
complaint, but if an investigation was initiated internally rather than
through complaint, it appeared in only the latter file. As a result our
tallies do not include internally initiated cases after April 9.

The two files list different issue descriptions to refer to the same cases,
and we utilized issue descriptions from both datasets in our analysis. For
example, “sexual violence” appears only in the complaint file descriptions,
while “discrimination against males” appears only in the investigation notices
file.
